blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The significance level (α) is the probability of a Type I error that the researcher accepts, fixed before the data are seen. Power (1 − β) is the probability that the test rejects H₀ when a specified true effect exists. An effect size is the magnitude of the effect or association being studied. A raw effect size is on the outcome’s own scale: a difference in means (kg), a risk difference, a risk ratio. A standardised effect size divides a difference by a standard deviation, which makes it unit-free; for two means it is Cohen’s d = (x̄₁ − x̄₂)/s_p, where s_p is the pooled SD, s_p = √{[(n₁ − 1)s₁² + (n₂ − 1)s₂²]/(n₁ + n₂ − 2)}.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: α is chosen by the researcher: “I accept rejecting a true H₀ this often, and no more.” Power is the other side of the Type II error rate: the chance that the study will find an effect of a stated size if it is there. Power always refers to a stated effect size, so the effect size must be defined first. A confidence interval is not an effect size. It is an interval estimate of an effect size, showing how precisely the effect has been measured.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Power of a two-sided z-test for a true difference Δ, when the estimate has standard error SE:

  1. Reject H₀ when the observed difference D lies beyond ±1.96 × SE.
  2. If the truth is Δ, then D is approximately normal with mean Δ and SD SE (recall §6.6), so (D − Δ)/SE is a standard normal Z.
  3. P(D > 1.96 SE) = P(Z > 1.96 − Δ/SE) = Φ(Δ/SE − 1.96). Here Φ(x) denotes the probability that a standard normal Z (recall §5.7.2.2.1) falls below x, read from normal tables or from any statistical software.
  4. The opposite tail adds Φ(−Δ/SE − 1.96), which is negligible once Δ/SE exceeds about 1.
  5. So power ≈ Φ(Δ/SE − 1.96). Power rises as Δ grows or SE shrinks.
  6. Reversing it: for equal groups of n with SD σ, SE = σ√(2/n). Setting Δ/SE = 1.96 + 0.84 (0.84 is the z-value with 80% below it) gives n = 2(1.96 + 0.84)²σ²/Δ² per group for 80% power. §15.6 (sample size for comparative studies) develops this.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
Urban–rural weights (recall §7.2.3: n₁ = 40, SD 2.0 kg; n₂ = 50, SD 1.8 kg; SE_diff = 0.406 kg).

  1. Raw effect size: 1 kg.
  2. Pooled SD: s_p = √[(39 × 2.0² + 49 × 1.8²)/88] = √[(156.0 + 158.8)/88] = √3.577 = 1.891 kg. Standardised effect size: d = 1/1.891 = 0.53.
  3. Power for a true 1 kg difference at α = 0.05: Δ/SE = 1/0.406 = 2.463; power = Φ(2.463 − 1.96) = Φ(0.503) = 0.69. So β = 0.31 (Figure 8.1).
  4. For a true 0.5 kg difference: Φ(0.5/0.406 − 1.96) = Φ(−0.73) = 0.23. The same study would miss a 0.5 kg difference more than three times in four.
  5. Doubling both groups (80 and 100): SE = √(4/80 + 3.24/100) = 0.287 kg, power for 1 kg = 0.94.
  6. Tightening α to 0.01 (cut-off 2.576) with the original groups: power for 1 kg = 0.46.
  7. Planning: equal groups with σ = 2 kg and Δ = 1 kg need n = 2 × 2.80² × 4/1 = 62.7 → 63 per group for 80% power. The slightly more exact calculation with the t-distribution, which software does, gives 63.8 → 64.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
se <- sqrt(2.0^2/40 + 1.8^2/50)     # SE of urban-rural difference
pnorm(1/se - qnorm(0.975))          # power, true difference 1 kg
power.t.test(delta = 1, sd = 2, power = 0.80)
[1] 0.6926441

     Two-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 63.76576
          delta = 1
             sd = 2
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number in *each* group

The first line is step 3: power 0.69 for a true 1 kg difference. power.t.test solves the planning question of step 7 using the t-distribution: 63.8, rounded up to 64 children per group, one more than the z-formula’s 63 because t has heavier tails (recall §5.7.2.3).

blocks.label: Common Misreading
blocks.html: “The result was not significant, so we calculated the power from our observed effect, and it was low.” This observed (post-hoc) power adds nothing. Put the observed z into the power formula and you get Φ(|z| − 1.96): a one-to-one function of the p-value. At p = 0.05, |z| = 1.96 and observed power is exactly 0.50; at p = 0.20 it is 0.25. Any result with p > 0.05 has observed power below about 50%, by arithmetic alone (Hoenig & Heisey, 2001; Greenland et al., 2016). Power is a planning quantity, computed before the study for an effect size chosen as clinically important. After the study, report the effect estimate with its confidence interval.

points.html: α = 0.05 is a convention. Fisher (1925) called P = 0.05 “convenient to take … as a limit”; it has been the usual default since (Cohen, 1992). Where many tests are run, stricter thresholds are used (§8.5).

80% power is a convention. Cohen (1992) proposed 0.80 “for general use”; ICH E9 notes that the Type II error is “conventionally” set at 10% to 20%, that is, power of 80% to 90% (ICH, 1998). Cohen also labelled d = 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 small, medium and large, but called these subjective conventions; a clinically important difference should be judged on the raw scale.
Power depends on four things: sample size, α, the true effect size and the variability of the data (together, Δ/SE and α). A larger n, a larger α, a larger effect or a smaller SD each raise power.

A non-significant result from a small study is ambiguous. There may be no effect, or the study may have been too small to detect one. The confidence interval shows which: a wide interval that includes clinically important effects means “inconclusive”, not “no effect”.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 8.1

questions.prompt: A small study reports “not statistically significant”, and adds that its observed power was 30%. Explain why this does not show there is no real effect, and why the observed power adds no information. What should the authors report instead?
questions.answer: Failing to reject H₀ is not proving it (§8.1). A small study has a large standard error, so it can miss a real, clinically important effect (a Type II error). The “observed power” is power computed at the observed effect: Φ(|z| − 1.96), a one-to-one function of the p-value. Every result with p > 0.05 has observed power below about 50%, so “30%” only restates “p was well above 0.05” (Hoenig & Heisey, 2001). The authors should report the effect estimate with its 95% confidence interval. If the interval includes clinically important effects, the study is inconclusive, not negative. Power belongs to the planning stage, for an effect size chosen in advance.

questions.prompt: Explain the trade-off between Type I and Type II error using a clinical example of your choosing. What, besides a larger sample, could reduce both?
questions.answer: Example: testing a new antihypertensive against H₀ “no effect”. A Type I error approves a useless drug; a Type II error abandons a useful one. For a fixed sample and design, lowering α (say from 0.05 to 0.01) moves the critical values outwards: fewer false approvals, more missed effects (in §8.4 power for a true 1 kg difference fell from 0.69 to 0.46). Both errors fall only if the standard error falls. Besides a larger n, a paired or matched design (each person as their own control) or a more precise measurement (less variability) lowers the SE and so reduces both.

questions.prompt: For the urban–rural comparison (SE_diff = 0.406 kg, pooled SD 1.891 kg), compute the standardised effect size d and the power for a true difference of 0.5 kg. How many children per group (σ = 2 kg, z-formula) would give 80% power for 0.5 kg?
questions.answer:
d = 0.5/1.891 = 0.26.

Power ≈ Φ(Δ/SE − 1.96) = Φ(0.5/0.406 − 1.96) = Φ(1.232 − 1.96) = Φ(−0.73) = 0.23. The study would miss a true 0.5 kg difference about 77% of the time.

n per group = 2(1.96 + 0.84)²σ²/Δ² = 2 × 7.84 × 4/0.25 = 250.9 → 251 per group (with the unrounded z-values, 1.95996 and 0.84162, 251.2 → 252; the t-distribution version, which software computes, gives 252.1 → 253). Halving the effect to be detected quadruples n (63 → about 251).
